data.q: What is Vite's primary advantage over traditional bundlers like Webpack during development?
o: It bundles all files into a single bundle before serving
It leverages native ES modules in the browser for instant server start
It compiles TypeScript to JavaScript ahead of time
It uses a custom module format for better caching
data.e: Vite serves source files via native ES modules, letting the browser handle imports on demand. This eliminates the need for a full bundle step on startup, making dev server start nearly instant.

data.q: Which Rust-based tool does Vite use for fast dependency pre-bundling?
o: swc
esbuild
turbopack
rolldown
data.e: Vite uses esbuild (written in Go, not Rust) to pre-bundle dependencies written in CommonJS or UMD into ESM, and to transform TypeScript/JSX quickly during dev.

data.q: What is the default command to start the Vite development server?
o: vite start
vite dev
vite serve
vite
data.e: Running `vite` (or `npx vite`) without a subcommand starts the dev server. `vite dev` is an alias, but the canonical command is just `vite`.

data.q: What is esbuild's primary design goal?
o: Maximum configurability
Extreme speed via parallelism and native code
Smallest output bundle size
Best TypeScript type checking
data.e: esbuild is written in Go and focuses on raw speed by parallelizing work across CPU cores and avoiding expensive AST transformations. It does not do type checking.

data.q: How does Vite handle module resolution differently in development versus production?
o: In dev it uses Rollup; in prod it uses esbuild
In dev it uses native ESM with on-demand compilation; in prod it bundles with Rollup
In dev it bundles everything; in prod it serves unbundled modules
There is no difference; Vite uses the same pipeline for both
data.e: During development Vite serves unbundled ESM and transforms files on demand. For production it uses Rollup to create optimized, bundled output with code splitting and minification.

data.q: What is the default port for the Vite development server?
data.e: Vite defaults to port 5173. If that port is busy, it will automatically try the next available port.

data.q: Which plugin API does Vite extend and remain compatible with?
o: Webpack plugin API
Rollup plugin API
esbuild plugin API
Parcel plugin API
data.e: Vite's plugin interface extends the Rollup plugin API, adding a few Vite-specific hooks (like `configureServer`). Most Rollup plugins work in Vite with little or no modification.

o: Bundles multiple files into a single output file
Compiles TypeScript/JSX to JavaScript and optionally minifies, without bundling
Runs a full production build with code splitting
Performs type checking on TypeScript files
data.e: The `transform` API takes a single source string, transpiles it (TS, JSX, modern JS) to target ES version, and can minify. It does not resolve imports or bundle.

data.q: How does Vite achieve fast Hot Module Replacement (HMR)?
o: By re-bundling the entire application on every change
By invalidating only the changed module chain via native ESM and sending minimal updates over WebSocket
By restarting the dev server on each file save
By using a custom binary protocol instead of WebSocket
data.e: Vite's HMR leverages native ESM: when a file changes, it invalidates that module and its importers, then requests the updated modules via HTTP. The browser swaps them in place without a full reload.

o: To define the entry point HTML file only
To configure Vite's behavior: plugins, server options, build options, resolve aliases, etc.
To store environment variables for the production build
To specify the TypeScript compiler options
data.e: `vite.config.js` is the central configuration file. It exports a config object (or a function returning one) that controls plugins, dev server, build output, CSS handling, resolve aliases, and more.

data.q: Which file does Vite use as the default entry point for the application?
o: src/main.js
index.html
src/App.vue
package.json
data.e: Vite is index-html-centric. The project root must contain an `index.html` file, which serves as the entry point. Scripts are referenced via `<script type="module" src="/src/main.js"></script>` inside it.

o: Enables minification of the output
Inlines all imported dependencies into a single output file
Generates source maps
Runs the TypeScript type checker
data.e: The `--bundle` flag tells esbuild to follow import/require statements and bundle all reachable modules into the output file(s). Without it, esbuild only transforms the entry file.

data.q: How does Vite handle TypeScript files by default?
o: It runs `tsc` for full type checking before serving
It uses esbuild to strip types and transpile to JavaScript, skipping type checking
It requires a separate `tsc --watch` process to compile .ts files to .js
It does not support TypeScript out of the box
data.e: Vite uses esbuild to transpile TypeScript (and TSX) to JavaScript by simply removing type annotations. It does not perform type checking during dev for speed; you should run `tsc --noEmit` separately or in CI.

data.q: What is the role of Rollup in Vite's production build?
o: It replaces esbuild for all transformations
It bundles the already esbuild-transformed modules into optimized production assets with code splitting, minification, and manifest generation
It serves the production build via a Node server
It only handles CSS extraction
data.e: For production, Vite uses Rollup (via `@vitejs/plugin-legacy` etc.) to create highly optimized bundles: code splitting, tree shaking, asset hashing, and HTML asset injection. esbuild is still used for fast transpilation during the build.

data.q: Which command creates a production-ready build in a Vite project?
o: vite build
vite prod
vite compile
vite bundle
data.e: `vite build` (or `npm run build` which typically maps to it) runs the production build using Rollup, outputting to the `dist` directory by default.

data.q: What is a key difference between esbuild and traditional bundlers like Webpack regarding plugins?
o: esbuild has a richer plugin API than Webpack
esbuild plugins are written in JavaScript and run in the same process
esbuild's plugin API is intentionally minimal and focuses on on-load/on-resolve hooks; it does not have a full compilation lifecycle like Webpack
esbuild does not support plugins at all
data.e: esbuild's plugin API is small: mainly `onResolve` and `onLoad` hooks. It lacks the extensive lifecycle hooks (e.g., chunk optimization, asset emission) that Webpack/Rollup provide, which is why Vite uses Rollup for production.
